content: The WHO Prequalification of In Vitro Diagnostics Programme is conducted following a structured process. The final outcome of the prequalification assessment depends on three key factors: the results of the dossier assessment and acceptance of any required corrective action plans, the results of inspections and acceptance of corrective action plans if needed, and meeting the minimum acceptance criteria during laboratory evaluations. WHO prioritizes applications for prequalification based on its prioritization criteria and programmatic suitability. It is also necessary to confirm whether the product is manufactured by the original manufacturer (not rebranded) and to identify the regulatory version of the product submitted. Products that have undergone stringent regulatory assessments by certain national authorities may qualify for an abbreviated WHO prequalification assessment, which still requires laboratory evaluation and a shortened inspection leveraging previous findings. A product dossier is a comprehensive document that demonstrates the in vitro diagnostic (IVD) device's compliance with essential safety and performance principles. WHO considers international best practices, such as guidance from the International Medical Device Regulators Forum (IMDRF) and standards from ISO and CLSI, to evaluate specialized areas like stability testing. The WHO prequalification assessment reviews the performance and use of IVDs, focusing on aspects such as stability, risk assessment, and instructions for use, specifically from the perspective of WHO Member States. Non-conformities identified during the review must be addressed by the manufacturer through a corrective action plan. The WHO inspection process for manufacturing sites involves several stages. Stage 1 evaluates readiness for inspection through a desktop review or brief on-site inspection. Stage 2 involves a full on-site inspection to assess the implementation of the quality management system, facilities, staff competence, critical suppliers, internal audits, and management commitment. Follow-up inspections confirm the implementation of corrective actions, while surveillance and re-inspections are conducted based on risk, with re-inspections occurring every 3–5 years. All inspected sites must meet prequalification requirements, including a fully implemented quality management system, risk management per ISO 14971, product stability, routine manufacturing, and sufficient capacity for reliable delivery. Independent laboratory evaluations of IVDs are conducted to assess performance and operational characteristics, such as sensitivity, specificity, and seroconversion sensitivity. Manufacturers provide one or two production lots to WHO-designated laboratories for testing. WHO issues a technical report on the assay's performance and determines if it meets prequalification requirements. Minimum acceptable performance criteria for serology assays include sensitivity >99% for rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and 100% for enzyme immunoassays (EIAs), specificity >98%, and low inter-reader variability and invalid rates. Operational characteristics of assays are also evaluated for suitability in resource-limited settings. For example, RDTs require minimal equipment and provide results within minutes, while EIAs require more equipment and have longer processing times. WHO issues a public report and adds prequalified products to its list, making them eligible for WHO and UN procurement. WHO may take actions such as exchanging surveillance information with regulatory authorities and manufacturers, publishing surveillance data, conducting additional surveillance, or removing products from the prequalified list if necessary. Quality control (QC) for HIV rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) involves monitoring the analytical performance of assays using test kit controls or external QC specimens. External QC specimens, such as low-reactive biological specimens, are prepared by diluting strongly reactive HIV-positive specimens in a suitable matrix. QC results should be recorded, analyzed, and monitored for trends that may require corrective actions. WHO is developing specific guidance on preparing QC specimens for RDTs. EQA can involve observational visits by trained supervisors or participation in proficiency testing programs using blinded specimen panels. Dried tube specimens (DTS) are a practical and cost-effective method for preparing specimens for distribution to testing sites. National reference laboratories should participate in international EQA schemes at least twice a year and conduct national EQA schemes using locally prepared DTS panels. WHO is preparing specific guidance on this topic.
